name: Steam-powered engine-shop tools
summary: The Soho double-acting steam engine was later connected to lathes and drills in Boulton and Watt's engine shops, using steam to power machine tools.
description: The same Soho double-reciprocating engine was subsequently applied to lathes and drills in the engine shops; Southern called it the boring engine.
tier_reason: A re-tasked installation is fine detail; the archive documents changed use, which is a legitimate event/role rather than a new general engine invention. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.

impact.note: One engine re-tasked to drive tools in one workshop, a local improvement with no later work shown to descend from it.

date.basis: Conversion occurred after the engine’s 1783 corn-mill use and before dismantling in 1803; the exact conversion year is unknown.

events.statement: The same Soho double-reciprocating engine was subsequently applied to lathes and drills in the engine shops; Southern called it the boring engine.
events.caveats: The conversion year, individual tools, and products made with them are not identified. No arrow back to the earlier Wilkinson machine is asserted.

evidence.supports: Reassignment from corn mill to engine-shop lathes/drills; Southern identification; dismantling in 1803.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. links.statement: The Soho engine was reassigned from corn milling to powering the engine shops' lathes and drills.
links.scope: Same named engine at Soho, after initial 1783 service and before dismantling in 1803.
links.alternatives: Water, manual labour and other prime movers could power tools; no universal dependence is asserted.
links.caveats: Precise conversion date and produced parts are unknown.
